worksheet.title: Off by One
worksheet.subtitle: Ontario Math C3.2 — read, find, and fix code
worksheet.learning_goal: I can fix a loop whose repeat number is one too many or too few.

parts.title: One too many or one too few
text: A very common bug is being OFF BY ONE — the repeat number is just one more or one less than it should be.
In a turtle shape, off by one is easy to see: a square needs range(4); range(3) leaves a side missing.

parts.caption: range(3) leaves the square open; range(4) closes it.

parts.title: Too many
parts.prompt: Bit should repeat 5 times, but the code says repeat 6. How many too many is that, and what should it be? ______

parts.title: Too few
parts.prompt: Bit should repeat 6 times, but the code says repeat 5. Is it too many or too few? What should it be?

parts.title: Fix the turtle
parts.prompt: This should draw a square:  for i in range(5): bit.forward(50); bit.right(90). The range is off by one. What should range() be?

parts.title: Challenge
parts.prompt: Bit's square code is  for i in range(3): bit.forward(50); bit.right(90). What does Bit draw now, and what one change fixes it? Explain why.

parts.title: Big idea
parts.text: Off-by-one is a tiny bug with a big effect. Always check the repeat number against the goal — one more or one less changes the whole result.

parts.title: What this worksheet teaches
parts.text: Students fix off-by-one loop bugs — a loop that repeats one too many or one too few — in both block (count) and shape (a square that does not close) cases. The method here is SHOULD → DOES → FIX: say what the code SHOULD do, run it to see what it DOES, then FIX the one thing that is wrong. No coding experience needed.

parts.title: Before you start
parts.text: No computer needed — the worksheet shows the code and what Bit should do. Optional: a Scratch-style app (for the block loops) or a free Python-turtle playground (for the shapes) to run the code — you only press Run.

parts.title: How to lead it (about 30 minutes)
text: 1. Show it (you do). A repeat that is one off makes Bit do one too many or one too few; for a shape, it leaves a side open.
2. Do one together. Exercise 1 — repeat 6 is one too many; fix to repeat 5.
3. Let them work. Students fix a too-few count (Ex 2), a square missing a side (Ex 3), and an open triangle-shape (Ex 4).

parts.title: Answer key (these are the verified correct answers)
text: Exercise 1 — one too many; repeat 5. Exercise 2 — too few; repeat 6.
Exercise 3 — repeat 4 times (a square has 4 sides). Exercise 4 (challenge) — only 3 sides are drawn (an open shape); change the repeat to 4 to close the square.

parts.title: If students get stuck — and ways to adjust
text: Watch for: fixing by a big jump. Off-by-one means change the count by just one.
Make it easier: count the sides the shape needs versus the sides it draws.
Make it harder: ask how an off-by-one looks different for a count versus a shape.

parts.title: Ontario curriculum link (official wording)
text: C3.1 — solve problems and create computational representations of mathematical situations by writing and executing code, including code that involves sequential, concurrent, and repeating events.
In plain terms: students write and run step-by-step instructions — including a "repeat" instruction — to make something happen.
C3.2 — read and alter existing code, including code that involves sequential, concurrent, and repeating events, and describe how changes to the code affect the outcomes.
In plain terms: students read instructions, find what is wrong, fix it, and explain what the change did.

parts.title: You'll know it worked when
parts.text: The child fixes the repeat by one so the count is right or the square closes.
